props.title: House
props.initialSlug: Seven schoolgirls face surreal horror in haunted house

sections.content: House (1977) is a psychedelic fever dream that demolishes every convention of horror cinema. Director Nobuhiko Obayashi unleashed a technicolor nightmare using experimental animation, surreal practical effects, and deliberately artificial visuals that feel like a haunted house designed by a sugar-rushing child. The film follows seven schoolgirls visiting a mysterious aunt's home, where they're picked off one-by-one in increasingly bizarre ways - from being eaten by a piano to getting devoured by hungry picture frames. It's the kind of unhinged creativity that influenced later genre-bending works like Evil Dead II (1987) and Hausu directly inspired the hyperactive style of modern filmmakers like Edgar Wright.

sections.content: The late 1970s Japanese film scene was exploding with experimental approaches that challenged traditional narrative. While House went the supernatural route, films like Lady Snowblood (1973) and Female Prisoner #701: Scorpion (1972) brought surreal, highly stylized violence to revenge tales. This era of Japanese cinema embraced excess and artificiality, rejecting the restraint of earlier decades. The influence extends to modern J-horror, with films like Uzumaki (2000) and Tag (2015) carrying on the tradition of reality-bending terror.

What makes House particularly revolutionary is how it melds innocence with horror. The cutesy schoolgirl tropes of Japanese pop culture crash headlong into genuine nightmare fuel. This combination of kawaii and horror later emerged in works like Perfect Blue (1997) and Happiness of the Katakuris (2001). The film's use of mixed media - combining animation, practical effects, and theatrical staging - created a template for genre-blending horror that continues today in films like Malignant (2021). sections.content: The DNA of House runs through countless modern films that blend horror with absurdist comedy. Cabin in the Woods (2011) directly references its "anything goes" approach to supernatural threats. The colorful violence of Suspiria (2018) owes a debt to Obayashi's technicolor bloodbaths. Even non-horror films like Scott Pilgrim vs. The World (2010) channel its rapid-fire visual style and gleeful disregard for reality.
